summary: A brief correction of several errors in RFC 567's bandwidth calculation. It notes, for example, that not all packets are 1000 bits long, and gives the actual sizes of RFNM messages and of Host-Host protocol messages.

plainLanguage.summary: A math homework about network traffic had mistakes. This note points out the wrong numbers and gives the right ones.

questions: how big is an arpanet rfnm
subtitle: BBN corrects the packet-size arithmetic in a claim about remote echo and cross-country bandwidth.

tldr.problem: RFC 567 claimed that remote character echoing could swamp cross-country network bandwidth, but McQuillan says it contains several fundamental errors.
tldr.mechanism: He gives the real sizes: a RFNM is 152 bits and a single-character Host-Host message is 216 bits, totalling 736 bits in each direction, not 4000.
tldr.outcome: The network can support over 200 single-character messages per second, not 37.5, and poor echo response is a delay problem rather than a bandwidth problem.

sections.title: What Was Wrong in RFC 567
sections.content: This note is a brief correction to several fundamental errors in RFC 567 by L. Peter Deutsch. The first is the assumption that all packets are 1000 bits long, which the author says is contrary to the basic network design.
sections.plainLanguage: The first mistake was thinking every parcel is the same size. They are not.

sections.title: The Corrected Numbers
sections.content:
RFNMs are 152 bits: 72 bits of hardware framing and 80 bits of software identification and addressing. Host-Host protocol messages such as single characters and allocates are 216 bits: 40 bits of Host protocol, 8 bits for the character or ALL, and 16 bits of IMP software header. The total is 736 bits in each direction, not 4000.

So the network can carry over 200 single-character messages per second, not 37.5. The note adds that such traffic is unlikely and is easier for the IMP subnetwork to support than for most Hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages were much smaller than the homework assumed, so many more fit through every second.

sections.title: Delay, Not Bandwidth
sections.content:
If demand for remote echoing ever exceeds capacity, TIPs and Hosts can buffer 2 characters per message to double the effective bandwidth, and dozens of characters can be packed into one message. This happens automatically as load rises and responses slow.

The author argues the more serious error is treating echo problems as bandwidth problems. They are delay problems. The IMP software uses a bimodal traffic model, with low delay for interactive traffic and high throughput for bulk transfers, and high data rates are pointless with short messages. As an extreme example, echoing over a megabit per second satellite link lags a second or more behind input with no bandwidth limit at all.

He agrees that changes to TELNET may well improve performance by reducing network traffic and Host processing, and calls them essential for long delay paths such as satellite links.
sections.plainLanguage: Slow typing echo is like a long drive to the mailbox, not a narrow road. A wider road would not help. Sending fewer, bigger trips would.

references.text: Deutsch, L. P., cross-country network bandwidth, RFC 567.
